newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ABARE boosts Australia 97/98 raw sugar to 5.66 MT.
newsitem.headline: ABARE boosts Australia 97/98 raw sugar to 5.66 MT.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) has increased its forecast for Australia's 1997/98 (July-June) raw sugar production to 5.66 million tonnes 94 net titre despite widespread destruction of the crop by cyclone Justin.
The forecast is up from 5.45 million tonnes in ABARE's March quarter forecast. The increase is based on an increase in harvest area, ABARE said.
In the area between Ingham and Mossman, which produces about 30 percent of the state of Queensland's sugarcane, loss of cane is estimated to have been 10 percent to 15 percent, it said.
Associated rain from the cyclone is also likely to reduce the sugar content of the cane and result in higher than usual harvesting, processing and replanting costs, ABARE said.
"Despite the losses, production in the northern region of Queensland is likely to fall by less than five percent in 1997/98 because of increased planting," it said.
For many growers from the Burdekin region and south, cyclone Justin provided much needed rain which should lead to increased yields, ABARE said.
ABARE also said world production of sugar is forecast to remain steady in 1997/98 after falling the year before.
European production is forecast to fall because of unfavourable weather and lower yields.
Offsetting this, production is expected to increase in South America and other regions, including Australia.
Production in India in 1998 is expected to be similar with the previous year.
But consumption in India continues to rise, stocks are expected to fall and there is a possibility that India could import some sugar in 1997/98, it said.
Chinese imports are likely to increase in 1997/98 after several years of declining imports and rising consumption, which have reduced stocks.
Brazilian exports are unlikely to rise in 1997/98, it said.
World sugar prices are forecast to fall to 10.7 U.S. cents a pound in 1997/98 from 11.2 cents a lb the year before as world stocks continue to rise, it said.
There was a 75 percent probability that the world sugar price would lie in a range of between 9.6 U.S. cents a lb and 11.6 cents in 1997/98, it said.
